Jobsite Safety: the Safety Plan, Hazards, PPE, Ladders and Lifts, Lockout

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 2 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The foreman says the ceiling above the corridor needs a pull tonight, and a ladder is already leaning on the wall. Before you climb, there are three things you owe the job: you have read the safety plan, you have reviewed the hazards in the space you are about to work, and you are wearing what the site requires.

Plan, review, protect

Verify and comply with the site safety plan. It lists the rules, the muster point, and who to call. A job hazard review walks the task step by step and asks what could hurt you at each step, then picks a control for it.

PPE item              When you wear it
Hard hat              under overhead work, on any active construction floor
Eye protection        drilling, cutting, stripping, and anything that makes chips or dust
Gloves                pulling, cutting, handling sharp metal edges
Hearing protection    coring, hammer drills, mechanical rooms
High-visibility vest  loading docks, parking, and any traffic area
Safety-toe boots      the whole shift on a construction site
Respirator            concrete dust and drywall dust

Ladders, lifts, and falls

Inspect the ladder before every use. Set it at a 4-to-1 pitch: the base sits 1 unit out for every 4 units of height. Keep three points of contact, face the ladder, and never stand on the top step of a stepladder or the top two rungs of an extension ladder. Extend an extension ladder 1 m (3.28 ft) above a landing so you can step on and off safely. A lift or scaffold needs training first, and fall protection is worn as the plan says.

Energy, air, and light

  • Lockout and tagout: installers never work on energized power. The person who controls the circuit locks and tags it.
  • Asbestos: if you suspect it, stop work, keep others away, and report it.
  • Silica dust comes from coring concrete: use water or a vacuum and wear a respirator.
  • Fiber: shards go in a sealed container, and you never look into a fiber end.
  • First aid: know the kit, report every injury, however small.

Every chemical on the job, from firestop sealant to pulling lubricant, comes with a safety data sheet that lists its hazards, the PPE it needs, and first aid; keep the sheets where the crew can reach them. A personnel lift, such as a scissor lift or a bucket lift, is used only after training, with the gate closed and a harness where the lift requires one. A powder-actuated tool fires a fastener into concrete or steel with a charge; only a trained, certified operator uses one, with eye and hearing protection.

Tip: a safe job is a quiet job. If you are about to improvise around a hazard, that is the moment to call the foreman.
Exam tip: the FIRST step before any hazardous task is to review the site safety plan and the hazards, not to start and fix problems as they appear.
Remember
Read the plan, review the hazards, wear the PPE, set the ladder at 4 to 1, never touch energized power, and stop on asbestos.
Deeper explanation

Jobsite Safety: the Safety Plan, Hazards, PPE, Ladders and Lifts, Lockout, explained slowly

Reading a hazard before you climb

A hazard review turns a vague worry into a short list of controls. You do it before the task, not after the near miss. The pattern is always the same: break the task into steps, name what could hurt you at each step, and pick the control.

Task step                  Hazard                    Control
Move ladder to corridor    strain, door swing        two people carry; block the door
Set the ladder             unstable base             4-to-1 pitch, level floor, foot support
Open the ceiling tile      dust, falling debris      eye protection, hard hat
Pull cable overhead        sharp edges, cuts         gloves
Drill a hole in a beam     chips, noise              glasses, hearing protection
Core a slab                silica dust               water, vacuum, respirator

The 4-to-1 ladder rule, worked

The base of an extension ladder sits 1 unit out for every 4 units of working height. A ladder that reaches 4 m up a wall has its base 1 m out. A ladder reaching 5 ft up has its base 1.25 ft out. Too steep and it tips backward; too shallow and the base slides out.

Worked example: you need to step off onto a 3.2 m (about 10.5 ft) landing. The ladder must extend 1 m (3.28 ft) above the landing, so the landing edge, where the ladder rests, is the 3.2 m working height. One quarter of 3.2 m puts the base 0.8 m from the wall. Always use three points of contact, face the ladder, and stay off the top step of a stepladder or the top two rungs of an extension ladder.

Energy control

Lockout and tagout is not a suggestion. If a task puts you near a circuit, the person who controls that circuit locks it and tags it. You never remove another worker's lock, and you never assume a panel is dead because it looks off. You are an installer, not an electrician, and power work belongs to the electrician.

Stop-work triggers

  • Suspected asbestos: stop, keep others away, report.
  • Unknown dust or fumes: stop and ask for the air to be checked.
  • A fiber end with a light source on: never look into it.
  • Any injury: report it, however small.
Remember: when a hazard has no control yet, the task waits. A late job is a smaller problem than a hurt installer.
